chapter: Touring, recording and Fletcher's band in the 1940s
title: Fletcher conducting: baton, shading and directed ad lib endings
summary: Fletcher loved directing with a baton and shading chords, and his charts with free intros and retards needed it, so he waved Horace to the piano mid-job.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: When he conducted, what was he actually doing? I mean, was he bringing in, like, you know, like the sax section and so on.

Different sections, (Inaudible) yes. And he used to have a little baton, and he was cute using it, and he had a little steps he'd do it from, you know. He would like this -- please believe it, Tom -- you know, he'd like to show off in front of the band, you know. He'd cut his little step, you know, cause the band would get to swingin', you get that beat, you get that feelin', you know. But most of all, getting back to the musical end of it, he was directing. He would like to draw the chords out, you know. He would have this little motion, you know, and the band would follow him. Shading, as we would call it. So he would like that. Well, he couldn't do it from the piano, and he got so he would love to see me walk in, you know. He'd call me right over there. Point.
Right in the middle of a job?
Right in the middle of a job, and sometimes he'd be broadcasting, and he would have to be up, you know, to cut the band off on certain notes, even if someone

-- you know, to come in, and then he would keep the beat going. would be singing (Inaudible). It required this, and he would make some intricate things in his arrangements that actually would require directing, because there weren't in tempo. Maybe an introduction would be an ad lib thing that needed conducting. Maybe somewhere to make the arrangement interesting, cause you know, on the ending. There might be a retard there, and then after the retard, the cut off, and then go back into tempo. Well, that's got to be directed.
-- to keep from being ragged, as we call it. So these are the things. And I liked this, because I knew later on it was gonna come in handy for me. So that was it. (TAPE 6)
